headline: New moon springs reopen the sunset flood bite at Execution Rocks and Stepping Stones
subhead: Bass are stacking on the PM tide as bunker pour past Matinecock and fluke abandon the warm harbors for deeper water.
body_markdown:
Last week the Sound did what it does every July — it got soft and sleepy in the middle of the day and came alive at the edges. Water in the harbors, Manhasset Bay and Hempstead Harbor especially, pushed well up into the mid-70s under a string of sunny, light-wind days, and that heat pushed the fluke right out of the shallow stuff and into the channels where they belong this time of year. Tide-wise we were riding out the back side of the June full moon cycle, so the current was still carrying some push through the week, but nothing dramatic — clean water, no real blow to speak of, and that let bait settle into its usual summer stations. Bunker schools have been thick off Matinecock Point on the last two hours of the incoming, and where you find bunker in July, you find blues and you find bass working underneath them.

This week the story is the new moon. We're building into new-moon springs through the weekend, with the tightest alignment falling July 11-13 — and that matters more than the moon phase itself. What it means practically is that Kings Point high stand is now lining up with sunset, which reopens the PM flood-sunset window for stripers for the first time since the June full moon cycle faded out. That's a real thing on this stretch of Sound — when the flood peaks right as the light goes down, bass move up onto the rockpiles and current breaks to feed in that low-light stretch before full dark, and Execution Rocks and Stepping Stones are ground zero for it. Bigger tide swings from the new moon also mean stronger current through the Throgs Neck rips and around Hart Island, which should reshuffle bait and put fish back on the reaction bite rather than the sluggish daytime pattern we've had.

On the striper side, it's been a mixed week honestly — not bad, but you had to work the tide stage right or you got nothing. The fish that are around Execution Rocks have been sitting tight to the rockpile on the last two hours of the outgoing, and the guys drifting bucktails — bone or white, 1 to 1.5 ounce, tipped with a strip of fresh bunker — have done the most damage in the 20 to 35 foot depths off the light. Live-lining bunker under a slip float around Stepping Stones on the early incoming has also produced, with a few fish pushing 30 inches, but you had to grind for them. The predictable window everyone should circle is the sunset flood I mentioned — Friday through Monday, July 10-13 — when that high stand at Kings Point lines up with dusk. That's when I'd be positioned on the up-current side of Execution Rocks with a swimming plug or a bunker chunk on a fish-finder rig, because that's the two-hour stretch where the bigger fish have been showing.

Bluefish have been the more consistent player. The bunker pods off Matinecock Point have blues underneath them most mornings on the tail of the incoming, and it's about as simple as fishing gets right now — heavy bunker spoons trolled through the edges of the school, or if you want to make it interesting, snag a bunker on a treble and freeline it back into the chaos. Choppers in the 3 to 6 pound range, occasional bigger fish mixed in. This bite tends to shut off hard once the sun gets up over the trees, so first light through about 8:30 is your window.

Fluke have shifted, same as I said above. Manhasset Bay and the mouth of Hempstead Harbor got too warm and too thin on bait, and the better fish have slid out to the channel edges and the deeper water toward Execution Rocks and the Throgs Neck approaches. Four-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow on the outgoing in 25 to 40 feet, have been the ticket — nothing gaudy, just a slow drag along bottom with occasional bumps to keep it in the strike zone. Sizes have been fair, mostly 16 to 19 inches with the occasional keeper mixed in, so it's not a bent-rod bonanza but it's a legitimate meal if you put in the drift time.

Porgies have been steady and honestly the most reliable thing going right now. The rockpiles at Execution Rocks and around Stepping Stones are holding good numbers, and a simple high-low rig with bloodworm or clam strips on size 6 or 4 hooks, fished tight to structure on a slowing tide, will fill a cooler without much drama. This is a good one to have in your back pocket on days when the bass and blues are being stubborn.

Weakfish, I'll be straight with you — quiet. Water's warm enough on paper, but I'm not hearing of real reports coming out of this end of the Sound, and I wouldn't plan a trip around them right now.

Looking ahead, the new-moon spring tides building into the weekend are the whole story for this zone. If that PM flood keeps lining up with sunset at Kings Point like the tide tables suggest, I'd be at Execution Rocks or Stepping Stones Friday through Monday evening, working the last two hours of the incoming into dark. If the bass don't cooperate on that stage, my backup is the Matinecock bunker school at first light — that bite has been the one sure thing all week, and with the tighter spring current pushing bait harder through the funnel points, I don't see any reason it slows down soon.
